questions.question: Which layer of the heart is composed of cardiac muscle tissue?

options.explanation: The endocardium is the inner lining of the heart, composed of endothelium and connective tissue.
The myocardium is the thick middle layer consisting of cardiac muscle cells responsible for contraction.
The epicardium is the outer layer, also called visceral pericardium.
The pericardium is the fibrous sac surrounding the heart, not the muscle layer.
The parietal pericardium lines the fibrous pericardium, not the heart wall.

explanation.overview: The heart wall has three layers: endocardium (inner), myocardium (middle muscle), and epicardium (outer).
explanation.highYield: Myocardium = cardiac muscle, contraction.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Myocarditis can impair pumping function.

questions.question: The endocardium is lined by:

options.explanation: The endocardium has an endothelial lining (simple squamous) over a subendothelial connective tissue layer.
Cuboidal epithelium is found in glands and kidney tubules.
Stratified squamous lines areas like the esophagus, not the heart.
Transitional epithelium is unique to the urinary system.
Pseudostratified columnar is typical of the respiratory tract.

explanation.overview: The endocardium is the inner lining of the heart chambers, consisting of endothelium and connective tissue.
explanation.highYield: Endocardium = simple squamous endothelium.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Endocardial damage can lead to thrombus formation.

questions.question: Which layer of a blood vessel is primarily responsible for vasoconstriction and vasodilation?

options.explanation: Tunica intima is the innermost layer, mainly endothelium and internal elastic lamina.
The tunica media contains concentric layers of smooth muscle that regulate vessel diameter.
The adventitia is the outer connective tissue layer, providing support.
The internal elastic membrane is a sheet of elastin, not muscle.
Endothelium lines the lumen but does not mediate contraction.

explanation.overview: Smooth muscle in the tunica media controls vascular tone and blood pressure.
explanation.highYield: Tunica media = smooth muscle, vasoconstriction/dilation.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Hypertension involves increased systemic vascular resistance.

questions.question: The internal and external elastic laminae are prominent in which type of artery?

options.explanation: Elastic arteries have multiple elastic lamellae, not distinct internal/external elastic laminae.
Muscular arteries have a prominent internal elastic lamina and often an external elastic lamina, demarcating the tunica media.
Arterioles have a thin internal elastic lamina but no external lamina.
Capillaries have no elastic laminae.
Venules lack elastic laminae.

explanation.overview: Muscular (distributing) arteries have well-defined internal and often external elastic laminae, separating layers.
explanation.highYield: Muscular artery: prominent internal + external elastic laminae.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Atherosclerosis often affects muscular arteries.

questions.question: Which vessel has the thickest tunica media relative to its lumen diameter?

options.explanation: Elastic arteries have a thick media but also a large lumen; relative thickness is less than muscular arteries.
Muscular arteries possess a very thick smooth muscle layer compared to their diameter.
Arterioles have a relatively thick media but the absolute thickness is lower.
Capillaries have no tunica media.
Venules have a thin media.

explanation.overview: Muscular arteries regulate blood flow to organs and have a dominant tunica media.
explanation.highYield: Muscular artery = thickest media proportionally.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Vasospasm of muscular arteries can cause ischemia.

questions.question: The tunica adventitia of veins is typically ______ than that of arteries.

options.explanation: Veins have a relatively thick adventitia with collagen and sometimes longitudinal smooth muscle.
Arteries generally have a thinner adventitia relative to the media.
They differ.
Veins have an adventitia.
Arteries have more elastic components.

explanation.overview: The adventitia is the dominant layer in veins, providing structural support.
explanation.highYield: Vein = thick adventitia, thin media.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Varicose veins occur when vein walls weaken.

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of capillaries?

options.text: Wall composed of endothelium, basal lamina, and pericytes
options.explanation: Capillaries consist of an endothelial tube, basal lamina, and occasional pericytes.

options.text: Presence of smooth muscle in the wall
options.explanation: Capillaries lack smooth muscle; it's found in larger vessels.
They have no tunica media.
Elastic laminae are not present in capillaries.
Valves are present in veins and lymphatics, not capillaries.

explanation.overview: Capillaries are the smallest blood vessels, facilitating exchange.
explanation.highYield: Capillary = endothelium + basal lamina + pericytes.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Pericyte loss is implicated in diabetic microangiopathy.

questions.question: Continuous capillaries are characterized by:

options.explanation: Continuous capillaries have a complete endothelial lining with tight intercellular junctions.
That describes fenestrated capillaries.
That's sinusoidal capillaries.
Continuous capillaries have a complete basal lamina.
Pores are in fenestrated capillaries.

explanation.overview: Continuous capillaries are the most common type, with uninterrupted endothelium and a continuous basal lamina.
explanation.highYield: Continuous capillary = tight junctions, complete basal lamina.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Blood-brain barrier is formed by continuous capillaries.

questions.question: Fenestrated capillaries are found in:

options.text: Glomeruli of kidney, intestinal villi, endocrine glands
options.explanation: Fenestrated capillaries with pores allow rapid exchange in these organs.
Those have sinusoidal capillaries.
Muscle has continuous capillaries.
Brain has continuous capillaries with tight junctions.
Lung capillaries are continuous.

explanation.overview: Fenestrated capillaries have pores (fenestrations) often closed by thin diaphragms.
explanation.highYield: Fenestrated capillaries = kidney, intestine, endocrine glands.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Glomerular capillaries are fenestrated without diaphragms.

questions.question: Sinusoidal (discontinuous) capillaries are characterized by:

options.text: Large intercellular gaps, discontinuous basal lamina
options.explanation: Sinusoids have wide, irregular lumens with gaps between endothelial cells and an incomplete basal lamina.
That's continuous capillaries.
Fenestrated capillaries have those.
Capillaries have no tunica media.
Pericytes may be present but sparse.

explanation.overview: Sinusoids are highly permeable capillaries found in organs that filter or process blood.
explanation.highYield: Sinusoid = large gaps, incomplete basal lamina (liver, spleen, bone marrow).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Hepatic sinusoids allow exchange of proteins and cells.

questions.question: Pericytes are cells associated with:

options.explanation: Pericytes (Rouget cells) are contractile cells surrounding endothelial cells of capillaries and venules.
Pericytes are not in large arteries.
Pericytes are not in large veins.
Lymphatic capillaries have sparse pericytes but are not the primary site.
Valves are avascular.

explanation.overview: Pericytes provide structural support and can regulate capillary diameter.
explanation.highYield: Pericytes = capillaries, post-capillary venules.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Pericyte dysfunction contributes to diabetic retinopathy.

questions.question: Which layer of the heart contains the Purkinje fibers?

options.explanation: Purkinje fibers run in the subendocardial connective tissue of the ventricles.
Purkinje fibers are located beneath the endocardium, not within the compact myocardium.
Epicardium is the outer layer.
Purkinje fibers are in the subendocardial layer, not the endothelial lining itself.
Pericardium is the sac around the heart.

explanation.overview: Purkinje fibers are modified cardiac muscle cells forming the terminal part of the ventricular conduction system.
explanation.highYield: Purkinje fibers = subendocardial location.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Damage to Purkinje fibers can cause bundle branch blocks.

questions.question: Purkinje fibers are histologically distinguished by:

options.text: Large, pale‑staining cells with sparse myofibrils and abundant glycogen
options.explanation: Purkinje cells are larger than working cardiomyocytes, pale due to glycogen, with few myofibrils.

options.text: Small, dark cells with densely packed myofibrils
options.explanation: That describes working cardiac muscle cells.
Purkinje cells are usually mononucleated and central.

options.text: Striated cells with prominent intercalated discs
options.explanation: Striations are less distinct due to sparse myofibrils.
They are still striated muscle.

explanation.overview: Purkinje fibers are modified for rapid impulse conduction.
explanation.highYield: Purkinje cells: large, pale, glycogen-rich, few myofibrils.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Easily identifiable on ventricular endocardial sections.

questions.question: The epicardium (visceral pericardium) consists of:

options.text: Mesothelium and fibroelastic connective tissue with adipose tissue
options.explanation: The epicardium has a mesothelial lining and underlying connective tissue often containing coronary vessels and fat.
Endothelium lines the endocardium, not epicardium.
It also contains adipose tissue.
Mesothelium is simple squamous, but the epicardium includes connective tissue.

options.text: Loose connective tissue with elastic fibers
options.explanation: Loose connective tissue is present but not the main descriptor.

explanation.overview: The epicardium is the visceral layer of the serous pericardium.
explanation.highYield: Epicardium = mesothelium + connective tissue + fat.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Coronary arteries run in the epicardial fat.

questions.question: The cardiac skeleton (fibrous skeleton) is composed of:

options.explanation: The fibrous skeleton consists of dense collagenous tissue forming rings around valves and septa.
No cartilage in the cardiac skeleton.
Not present.
The cardiac skeleton is not bone.
It is connective tissue, not muscle.

explanation.overview: The cardiac skeleton anchors valves, provides electrical insulation, and maintains cardiac shape.
explanation.highYield: Cardiac skeleton = dense irregular connective tissue.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Calcification of the fibrous skeleton can affect valve function.

questions.question: Which vessels are characterized by the presence of valves?

options.text: Veins, especially in the lower limbs
options.explanation: Valves are intimal folds that prevent retrograde flow in veins, particularly those against gravity.
Arteries do not have valves; blood flow is maintained by pressure.
Capillaries lack valves.
Arterioles regulate flow but have no valves.
Lymphatics also have valves, but the question specifies 'vessels' and the classic answer is veins.

explanation.overview: Venous valves are formed by folds of tunica intima, preventing backflow.
explanation.highYield: Valves = veins (especially lower limb) and lymphatics.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Valve incompetence leads to varicose veins.

questions.question: The vasa vasorum are:

options.text: Small vessels that supply the walls of large arteries and veins
options.explanation: Vasa vasorum are microvessels that penetrate the adventitia and outer media of large vessels.
Myocardial vessels are coronary capillaries.
Lymphatics are not vasa vasorum.
Those are nervi vasorum.
Not smooth muscle cells.

explanation.overview: Vasa vasorum ('vessels of the vessels') nourish thick vessel walls.
explanation.highYield: Vasa vasorum = small arteries/veins in wall of large vessels.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Impaired vasa vasorum flow contributes to aortic aneurysms.

questions.question: Which type of arteriole is most important in regulating systemic blood pressure?

options.explanation: All arterioles are resistance vessels.
Metarterioles are a subset.
Sphincters control local flow, not systemic pressure.
Arterioles collectively are the major resistance vessels determining peripheral resistance.
Elastic arteries dampen pressure, not primarily regulate resistance.

explanation.overview: Systemic vascular resistance is mainly determined by the tone of arterioles.
explanation.highYield: Arterioles = resistance vessels → blood pressure.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Antihypertensive drugs often target arteriolar smooth muscle.

questions.question: A metarteriole is a vessel that:

options.text: Connects an arteriole directly to a venule (thoroughfare channel)
options.explanation: Metarterioles are terminal arterioles that can bypass capillary beds via thoroughfare channels.

options.text: Has a continuous smooth muscle layer
options.explanation: Metarterioles have discontinuous smooth muscle.

options.text: Is always surrounded by precapillary sphincters
options.explanation: Precapillary sphincters are at the origin of capillaries from metarterioles.

options.text: Is another name for a capillary
options.explanation: It's larger and has some smooth muscle.

options.text: Is found only in the liver
options.explanation: Metarterioles are widespread, e.g., mesentery.

explanation.overview: Metarterioles link arterioles to venules and regulate microcirculatory flow.
explanation.highYield: Metarteriole = thoroughfare channel, bypasses capillaries.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Shunt pathways can redirect blood away from exchange areas.

questions.question: Precapillary sphincters are located at the origin of:

options.explanation: Precapillary sphincters are rings of smooth muscle at the entrance of capillaries, controlling blood flow.
Not the site.
Post‑capillary side.
Lymphatics lack these sphincters.
Shunts are direct arteriole‑venule connections.

explanation.overview: Precapillary sphincters regulate perfusion of individual capillary beds.
explanation.highYield: Precapillary sphincter = smooth muscle at capillary origin.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Relaxation increases blood flow to metabolically active tissues.

questions.question: Arteriovenous anastomoses (shunts) allow blood to bypass:

options.explanation: Direct connections between arterioles and venules divert blood away from capillaries.
They are part of the arteriole‑venule connection.
They connect to venules.
Not relevant.
Not relevant.

explanation.overview: AV shunts are important in thermoregulation, especially in skin.
explanation.highYield: AV shunts = bypass capillaries, thermoregulation.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Glomus tumors arise from modified AV shunts.

questions.question: Which cell type lines the lumen of all blood and lymphatic vessels?

options.explanation: Endothelium is the simple squamous epithelium that lines the entire cardiovascular system.
Smooth muscle is in the vessel wall, not the lining.
Fibroblasts are in the connective tissue.
Pericytes surround capillaries externally.
Mesothelium lines body cavities, not vessel lumens.

explanation.overview: Endothelial cells form a continuous, semipermeable barrier.
explanation.highYield: All vessels lined by endothelium.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Endothelial injury initiates atherosclerosis.

questions.question: Weibel‑Palade bodies are storage granules found in endothelial cells that contain:

options.explanation: Weibel‑Palade bodies are rod‑shaped organelles specific to endothelial cells, storing vWF and P‑selectin.
Histamine is in mast cell and basophil granules.
Heparin is in mast cell granules.
NO is a soluble gas, not stored in granules.
Endothelin is not stored in Weibel‑Palade bodies.

explanation.overview: Weibel‑Palade bodies are the diagnostic ultrastructural feature of endothelial cells.
explanation.highYield: Weibel‑Palade body = vWF + P‑selectin (endothelium marker).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: vWF deficiency causes von Willebrand disease.

questions.question: Which of the following is a function of endothelial cells?

options.explanation: Part of endothelial function.
Endothelium produces vasodilators (NO) and vasoconstrictors (endothelin).
Endothelium provides anticoagulant surface and releases clotting factors.
Endothelial cells proliferate to form new vessels.
Endothelium has multiple roles: barrier, regulation of tone, hemostasis, and angiogenesis.

explanation.overview: Endothelium is a dynamic, multifunctional organ.
explanation.highYield: Endothelium functions: barrier, vasoregulation, hemostasis, angiogenesis.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Endothelial dysfunction is a precursor to atherosclerosis.

questions.question: The tunica intima of an artery consists of:

options.text: Endothelium, subendothelial connective tissue, and internal elastic lamina
options.explanation: The intima is the innermost layer, with endothelium, a thin subendothelial layer, and (in arteries) a distinct internal elastic lamina.
That's the tunica media.
That's tunica adventitia.
It also contains subendothelial connective tissue.
Smooth muscle is in media.

explanation.overview: The tunica intima includes the endothelial lining and internal elastic lamina (where present).
explanation.highYield: Tunica intima = endothelium + subendothelium + IEL.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Atherosclerotic plaques develop in the intima.

questions.question: In elastic arteries (e.g., aorta), the tunica media contains:

options.text: Multiple concentric elastic lamellae with smooth muscle
options.explanation: Elastic arteries have numerous fenestrated elastic lamellae interspersed with smooth muscle cells.

options.text: Dense smooth muscle with little elastin
options.explanation: That describes muscular arteries.
Collagen is mainly in adventitia.
Media has smooth muscle and elastin.
No.

explanation.overview: Elastic arteries store energy during systole and recoil during diastole.
explanation.highYield: Elastic artery media = elastic lamellae + smooth muscle.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Loss of elasticity leads to systolic hypertension.

questions.question: The aorta is classified as:

options.explanation: The aorta is the largest elastic artery, with abundant elastin in its wall.
Muscular arteries are distributing arteries.
Arterioles are small resistance vessels.
Capillaries are microscopic exchange vessels.
Veins return blood to the heart.

explanation.overview: Elastic arteries receive blood directly from the heart.
explanation.highYield: Aorta = elastic artery.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Aortic aneurysm involves dilation of the elastic wall.

questions.question: Compared to arteries, veins have:

options.text: Larger lumen, thinner wall, and less elastic tissue
options.explanation: Veins are capacitance vessels with a larger diameter, thinner wall, and fewer elastic fibers.

options.text: Smaller lumen, thicker wall, and more smooth muscle
options.explanation: That's arteries.
Internal elastic lamina is more prominent in arteries.
Elastic lamellae are in arteries.
Veins have larger lumen.

explanation.overview: Veins are distensible, low‑pressure vessels.
explanation.highYield: Vein = large lumen, thin wall, little elastin.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Veins can accommodate large blood volumes.

questions.question: Venules are post‑capillary vessels that:

options.text: Are important sites of leukocyte extravasation
options.explanation: Post‑capillary venules are the primary sites where leukocytes exit the circulation during inflammation.
Venules have thin walls with little smooth muscle.
Valves appear in larger veins.
They are lined by endothelium (squamous).

options.text: Have a well‑developed internal elastic lamina
options.explanation: Elastic laminae are absent in venules.

explanation.overview: Post‑capillary venules are key in the inflammatory response.
explanation.highYield: Venule = leukocyte extravasation site.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Venulitis can occur in various vasculitides.

questions.question: Cardiac muscle cells are joined end‑to‑end by specialized intercellular junctions called:

options.explanation: Intercalated discs are complex junctions containing fascia adherens, desmosomes, and gap junctions.
Gap junctions are one component of intercalated discs.
Desmosomes are also components.
Tight junctions are not present in intercalated discs.
Intercalated discs contain fascia adherens, desmosomes, and gap junctions, not tight junctions.

explanation.overview: Intercalated discs enable mechanical and electrical coupling.
explanation.highYield: Intercalated disc = fascia adherens + desmosomes + gap junctions.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Disruption of gap junctions can cause arrhythmias.

questions.question: The transverse portion of an intercalated disc contains:

options.explanation: The transverse segment has fascia adherens for actin attachment and desmosomes for mechanical strength.
Gap junctions are mainly in the lateral portion.
Tight junctions are not present.
Hemidesmosomes attach cells to basal lamina.
Desmosomes are also present.

explanation.overview: The intercalated disc has transverse (mechanical) and lateral (electrical) domains.
explanation.highYield: Transverse disc = fascia adherens + desmosomes.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Mutations in desmosomal proteins cause arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy.

questions.question: Gap junctions in cardiac muscle are primarily located in the:

options.explanation: Gap junctions are concentrated in the lateral segments, allowing rapid ion passage.
Transverse portions have fascia adherens and desmosomes.
T‑tubules are membrane invaginations.
SR stores calcium.
Z discs anchor actin.

explanation.overview: Gap junctions provide electrical continuity, forming a functional syncytium.
explanation.highYield: Gap junctions = lateral portions of intercalated disc.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Connexin mutations can cause conduction defects.

questions.question: Which of the following is a histological difference between cardiac and skeletal muscle?

options.text: Cardiac muscle cells are branched and have central nuclei
options.explanation: Cardiac myocytes are branched, uninucleate (usually), with central nuclei.
Cardiac muscle is striated.

options.text: Cardiac muscle has multiple peripheral nuclei
options.explanation: Skeletal muscle has multiple peripheral nuclei.
Intercalated discs are unique to cardiac muscle.
Skeletal muscle is voluntary.

explanation.overview: Cardiac muscle is involuntary, striated, branched, with central nuclei and intercalated discs.
explanation.highYield: Cardiac muscle = branched, central nucleus, intercalated discs.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Myocardial infarction results in irreversible loss of cardiomyocytes.

questions.question: The conducting system of the heart includes all of the following EXCEPT:

options.explanation: SA node is part of the conduction system.
AV node is part.
Bundle of His is part.
Purkinje fibers are part.
Working (contractile) cardiomyocytes are not part of the specialized conduction system.

explanation.overview: The conduction system includes specialized cells for impulse generation and propagation.
explanation.highYield: Conduction system = SA node, AV node, bundle of His, Purkinje.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Dysfunction can cause heart block.

questions.question: The sinoatrial (SA) node is located in the:

options.text: Right atrium near the entrance of the superior vena cava
options.explanation: The SA node is a subepicardial structure at the junction of the right atrium and SVC.
Not in the left atrium.
The AV node is near the interatrial septum.
AV node is at the junction.
Bundle branches are in the septum.

explanation.overview: The SA node is the primary pacemaker.
explanation.highYield: SA node = right atrium + SVC junction.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Sick sinus syndrome requires pacemaker.

questions.question: Histologically, the SA node consists of:

options.text: Small, pale‑staining nodal cells (P cells) embedded in fibrous stroma
options.explanation: Nodal (P) cells are small, have few myofibrils, and are surrounded by dense connective tissue.
Purkinje cells are larger and located in ventricles.
SA node cells are modified.
It's cardiac muscle, not smooth.
Contains nodal cells and connective tissue.

explanation.overview: P (pacemaker) cells generate spontaneous impulses.
explanation.highYield: SA node = small pale P cells + fibrous tissue.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Fibrosis of SA node can cause bradycardia.

questions.question: Which type of capillary is found in the renal glomerulus?

options.explanation: Glomerular capillaries are fenestrated without diaphragms.
The fenestrations in glomerular capillaries lack diaphragms, allowing high permeability.
Continuous capillaries are elsewhere.
Sinusoids are in liver, spleen.
Similar to sinusoidal but not the glomerulus.

explanation.overview: Glomerular capillaries are uniquely fenestrated without diaphragms.
explanation.highYield: Glomerulus = fenestrated, no diaphragms.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Proteinuria indicates damage to filtration barrier.

questions.question: Which of the following vessels is lined by endothelium with tight junctions that form the blood‑brain barrier?

options.explanation: CNS capillaries have continuous endothelium with tight junctions, forming the blood‑brain barrier.
Fenestrated capillaries are more permeable.
Sinusoids have large gaps.
Lymphatics are not in CNS parenchyma.
Venules do not form the BBB.

explanation.overview: Continuous capillaries with tight junctions restrict paracellular transport.
explanation.highYield: Blood‑brain barrier = continuous capillaries + tight junctions.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Disruption of BBB occurs in inflammation, stroke.

questions.question: Lymphatic capillaries differ from blood capillaries by:

options.text: Absence of a continuous basal lamina and presence of anchoring filaments
options.explanation: Lymphatic capillaries have an incomplete basal lamina and are attached by anchoring filaments to the ECM.

options.text: Presence of a thick tunica media
options.explanation: Capillaries have no media.
Both are lined by endothelium.
Valves are in larger lymphatics, not capillaries.
Lymphatics typically lack RBCs.

explanation.overview: Lymphatic capillaries are more permeable due to their structure.
explanation.highYield: Lymphatic capillary: no continuous basal lamina, anchoring filaments.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Tumor cells can invade lymphatic capillaries.

questions.question: The subendocardial layer of the heart contains:

options.text: Purkinje fibers, blood vessels, and nerves
options.explanation: The subendocardium is loose connective tissue beneath the endocardium that houses the conduction system and small vessels.
Cardiac muscle is in the myocardium.
Adipose tissue may be present in epicardium.
Serous lining is the epicardium.
Valves are extensions of the fibrous skeleton.

explanation.overview: Subendocardial layer is the innermost myocardial region.
explanation.highYield: Subendocardium = Purkinje fibers, vessels, nerves.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Ischemia often affects subendocardium first.

questions.question: Which heart valve is typically thicker and may contain a small amount of cardiac muscle at its base?

options.explanation: AV valves are thicker, attached to papillary muscles, and may have a small amount of ventricular myocardium extending into the base.
Semilunar valves are thinner and lack chordae tendineae.
They differ.
No.
Both mitral and tricuspid are AV valves.

explanation.overview: AV valves have chordae tendineae and papillary muscle connections.
explanation.highYield: AV valves = thicker, cardiac muscle at base possible.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Papillary muscle rupture causes acute mitral regurgitation.

questions.question: Chordae tendineae are composed of:

options.explanation: Chordae tendineae are fibrous cords that connect papillary muscles to AV valve cusps.
Not primarily elastic.
No smooth muscle.
Papillary muscle is cardiac, but chordae are fibrous.
No.

explanation.overview: Chordae tendineae are collagenous cords that prevent valve prolapse.
explanation.highYield: Chordae = dense collagen.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Rupture leads to valve regurgitation.

questions.question: Papillary muscles are part of the:

options.explanation: Papillary muscles are projections of ventricular myocardium.
Endocardium covers them but they are muscular.
Epicardium is the outer layer.
Valves are fibrous.
Fibrous skeleton is connective tissue.

explanation.overview: Papillary muscles contract to tense chordae tendineae during ventricular systole.
explanation.highYield: Papillary muscle = myocardium.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Ischemia can cause papillary muscle dysfunction.

questions.question: The cardiac skeleton (fibrous rings) electrically insulates the atria from the ventricles except at the:

options.explanation: The only normal conduction pathway through the fibrous skeleton is the AV bundle.
SA node is in the atrium.
AV node is above the skeleton; the bundle penetrates it.
Purkinje fibers are in ventricles.
Not the electrical connection.

explanation.overview: The fibrous skeleton prevents direct electrical spread from atria to ventricles.
explanation.highYield: Only electrical connection: AV bundle (bundle of His).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Accessory pathways (WPW syndrome) bypass the skeleton.

questions.question: Which cells are responsible for phagocytosis in the spleen's red pulp?

options.explanation: Macrophages in the splenic cords phagocytose aged erythrocytes and pathogens.
Endothelial cells line sinuses but don't phagocytose.
Lymphocytes are in white pulp.
Not phagocytic.
Dendritic cells are in white pulp.

explanation.overview: The splenic red pulp filters blood and removes old RBCs.
explanation.highYield: Red pulp macrophages = RBC phagocytosis.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Splenectomy increases Howell-Jolly bodies.

questions.question: The splenic white pulp consists mainly of:

options.text: Lymphocytes (periarteriolar lymphatic sheaths and lymphoid follicles)
options.explanation: White pulp is lymphoid tissue surrounding central arteries.
Macrophages are in the marginal zone and red pulp.
Erythrocytes are in red pulp.
Fibroblasts are in trabeculae.
Plasma cells may be in red pulp, not primarily white pulp.

explanation.overview: White pulp is the immunologically active region of the spleen.
explanation.highYield: White pulp = PALS (T cells) + follicles (B cells).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Splenic white pulp hyperplasia in infections.

questions.question: The marginal zone of the spleen contains:

options.text: Macrophages and specialized B cells that respond to blood‑borne antigens
options.explanation: The marginal zone at the white‑red pulp interface is rich in macrophages and marginal zone B cells.
T cells are mainly in PALS.
Red pulp contains RBCs.
Trabeculae are supportive structures.
Central arterioles are in white pulp.

explanation.overview: The marginal zone is a critical area for immune surveillance of blood.
explanation.highYield: Marginal zone = macrophages + marginal zone B cells.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Marginal zone B cells mediate T‑independent responses.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the structure of a lymph node?

options.text: Cortex with follicles, paracortex, medulla with medullary cords and sinuses
options.explanation: Lymph node: outer cortex (B cells), paracortex (T cells), medulla with cords (plasma cells) and sinuses.
That's spleen.
Lymph nodes have a sinus system.
That's spleen white pulp.
That's intestine.

explanation.overview: Lymph nodes filter lymph and provide an environment for adaptive immunity.
explanation.highYield: Lymph node = cortex (B), paracortex (T), medulla (cords/sinuses).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Lymphadenopathy indicates immune activation or malignancy.

questions.question: High endothelial venules (HEV) are found in:

options.text: Paracortex of lymph nodes and tonsils
options.explanation: HEVs are specialized post‑capillary venules with cuboidal endothelium that facilitate lymphocyte entry into lymphoid organs.
Spleen uses different mechanisms.
Thymus has blood‑thymus barrier, not classic HEVs.
Not in bone marrow.
Sinusoids are different.

explanation.overview: HEVs are the gateway for lymphocyte homing to lymph nodes and MALT.
explanation.highYield: HEVs = lymph node paracortex, tonsils, Peyer's patches.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: HEV‑like vessels form in chronic inflammation.

questions.question: The thymus is characterized by the presence of:

options.text: Hassall's corpuscles (thymic corpuscles) in the medulla
options.explanation: Hassall's corpuscles are concentric whorls of keratinized epithelial cells unique to the thymic medulla.
Germinal centers are in lymph nodes and spleen, not normal thymus.
Spleen.
Tonsils have crypts.
HEVs are not prominent in thymus; cortex has blood‑thymus barrier.

explanation.overview: Hassall's corpuscles are diagnostic for thymus.
explanation.highYield: Thymus = Hassall's corpuscles in medulla.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Thymomas often contain Hassall's corpuscles.

questions.question: Which type of muscle is found in the tunica media of blood vessels?

options.explanation: The tunica media contains smooth muscle cells that regulate vessel diameter.
Cardiac muscle is only in the heart.
Skeletal muscle is voluntary and not in vessel walls.
Myoepithelial cells are in glands.
Pericytes are in capillaries, not the media of larger vessels.

explanation.overview: Smooth muscle in the tunica media allows vasoconstriction and vasodilation.
explanation.highYield: Vascular smooth muscle = tunica media.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Vascular smooth muscle proliferation occurs in atherosclerosis and hypertension.

questions.question: Which of the following is true of lymphatic vessels?

options.text: They possess valves and a discontinuous basal lamina in capillaries
options.explanation: Lymphatic capillaries have anchoring filaments and an incomplete basal lamina; larger lymphatics have valves.
They have thinner walls and more valves.

options.text: They carry blood back to the heart
options.explanation: They carry lymph.

options.text: They contain smooth muscle in the capillary walls
options.explanation: Lymphatic capillaries lack smooth muscle.

options.text: They have a thick tunica media
options.explanation: They have a relatively thin wall.

explanation.overview: Lymphatic system returns interstitial fluid and immune cells.
explanation.highYield: Lymphatics: valves, incomplete basal lamina in capillaries.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Lymphedema occurs when lymphatics are obstructed.

questions.question: The major structural difference between an artery and a vein is the:

options.text: Thickness of the tunica media relative to the lumen
options.explanation: Arteries have a thick media; veins have a thinner media and larger lumen.
Both have endothelium.
Both have elastic fibers, though more in arteries.

options.text: Type of epithelium lining the lumen
options.explanation: Both are lined by simple squamous endothelium.
Both have collagen in adventitia.

explanation.overview: Arteries are thicker-walled with a prominent media; veins are capacitance vessels.
explanation.highYield: Artery = thick media; vein = thin media, large lumen.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Venous grafts used in bypass surgery may fail due to arterial pressure.

questions.question: Which of the following is a component of the blood‑thymus barrier?

options.text: Thymic epithelial cells with tight junctions, basal lamina, and endothelial cells
options.explanation: The blood‑thymus barrier in the cortex shields developing T cells from antigens.
HEVs are in lymph nodes, not thymus.
Hassall's corpuscles are in medulla, not barrier.
Not part of the barrier.
Reticular fibers support but are not the barrier.

explanation.overview: The blood‑thymus barrier prevents premature exposure of developing T cells to antigens.
explanation.highYield: Blood‑thymus barrier = epithelial reticular cells + basal lamina + endothelium.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Disruption may lead to autoimmunity.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the structure of a muscular artery?

options.text: Prominent internal and external elastic laminae, thick smooth muscle media
options.explanation: Muscular arteries have a well‑defined internal elastic lamina, a thick muscular media, and often an external elastic lamina.
That's elastic artery.

options.text: Only endothelium and a thin adventitia
options.explanation: That's capillary/venule.
Endothelium is continuous in arteries.
They have abundant smooth muscle.

explanation.overview: Muscular (distributing) arteries control blood flow to organs.
explanation.highYield: Muscular artery: prominent IEL, EEL, thick smooth muscle.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: These are common sites for atherosclerosis.

questions.question: The endocardium is analogous to which layer of a blood vessel?

options.explanation: The endocardium is the inner lining, similar to the tunica intima of vessels.
Media contains smooth muscle, not present in endocardium.
Adventitia is outer connective tissue.
A specific layer, not the entire endocardium.
Pericardium is external.

explanation.overview: The endocardium and tunica intima both comprise endothelium and subendothelial connective tissue.
explanation.highYield: Endocardium ↔ tunica intima.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Endocarditis involves inflammation of this inner layer.

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of cardiac muscle under electron microscopy?

options.text: Numerous mitochondria, centrally placed nucleus, intercalated discs
options.explanation: Cardiac myocytes are rich in mitochondria (to sustain continuous contraction), have a central nucleus, and are joined by intercalated discs.
Skeletal muscle has peripheral nuclei; cardiac has central nuclei and many mitochondria.
Cardiac muscle is striated.
It is striated.
Cardiac cells are branched and usually mononucleated.

explanation.overview: Cardiac muscle is designed for endurance and coordinated contraction.
explanation.highYield: Cardiac EM: many mitochondria, central nucleus, intercalated discs.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Myocardial infarction leads to necrosis with loss of these features.

questions.question: The subendocardial Purkinje fibers are most abundant in which part of the heart?

options.explanation: Purkinje fibers are extensive in the subendocardium of the ventricles, especially near the septum and papillary muscles.
They are not in atria.
They are beyond the AV node.
No Purkinje fibers in SA node.
They are subendocardial, not epicardial.

explanation.overview: Purkinje fibers rapidly spread the impulse through the ventricles.
explanation.highYield: Purkinje fibers: subendocardial, ventricular septum, papillary muscles.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Purkinje fiber damage can cause intraventricular conduction delay.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about the pulmonary artery compared to systemic arteries?

options.text: It is an elastic artery but has a thinner wall than the aorta
options.explanation: The pulmonary artery is an elastic artery, but because pulmonary pressure is lower, its wall is thinner than the aorta.
It is classified as elastic.
It has elastic lamellae, just fewer.
It carries deoxygenated blood but is an artery.

options.text: It has a thicker wall than the aorta
options.explanation: The aortic wall is thicker.

explanation.overview: Pulmonary arteries are elastic, adapted to low-resistance pulmonary circulation.
explanation.highYield: Pulmonary artery: elastic, thinner wall than aorta.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Pulmonary hypertension causes medial hypertrophy.

questions.question: In the spleen, the central arterioles are surrounded by:

options.explanation: Central arterioles are surrounded by T‑cell‑rich PALS, part of white pulp.
Red pulp is outside white pulp.
Marginal zone surrounds PALS/follicles.
Sinuses are in red pulp.
Trabeculae are fibrous bands.

explanation.overview: PALS is the T‑cell domain of the white pulp.
explanation.highYield: Central arteriole → PALS (T cells).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: In HIV, PALS is depleted.

questions.question: The internal elastic lamina is best visualized with which stain?

options.explanation: Verhoeff stain colors elastin black, making the internal elastic lamina prominent.
H&E shows it as a refractile line but not specific.
Trichrome stains collagen and muscle.
PAS stains carbohydrates.
Stains lipids.

explanation.overview: Elastic fibers are demonstrated by special stains like Verhoeff, orcein, or resorcin-fuchsin.
explanation.highYield: Elastin stain: Verhoeff (black).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Fragmentation of IEL is seen in temporal arteritis.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of continuous capillaries?

options.explanation: Fenestrations are absent in continuous capillaries; they are present in fenestrated capillaries.
Continuous capillaries have tight junctions.
They have a complete basal lamina.
Pericytes are present.
Vesicles are present for transcytosis.

explanation.overview: Continuous capillaries lack fenestrations and have continuous endothelium and basal lamina.
explanation.highYield: Continuous = no fenestrations, tight junctions, complete lamina.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Found in muscle, lung, brain.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about the tunica adventitia?

options.text: It is the outermost layer, composed of loose connective tissue with collagen and elastic fibers
options.explanation: The adventitia blends with surrounding connective tissue and contains vasa vasorum in larger vessels.

options.text: It contains smooth muscle as its main component
options.explanation: Smooth muscle is in the media.
Mesothelium lines serous cavities.
Veins have a prominent adventitia.

options.text: It contains the internal elastic lamina
options.explanation: Internal elastic lamina is between intima and media.

explanation.overview: The adventitia anchors vessels and provides structural integrity.
explanation.highYield: Adventitia = outermost, collagen, vasa vasorum.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Inflammation of adventitia occurs in vasculitis.

questions.question: The splenic red pulp consists of:

options.text: Cords of Billroth and splenic sinusoids
options.explanation: Red pulp is a meshwork of reticular fibers, macrophages, and blood-filled sinusoids.
White pulp is lymphoid tissue.
Follicles are in white pulp.
Those are in thymus.
HEVs are in lymph nodes.

explanation.overview: Red pulp filters blood, removing aged erythrocytes.
explanation.highYield: Red pulp = cords + sinusoids.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Splenomegaly involves expansion of red pulp.

questions.question: Which of the following is a modified smooth muscle cell that can contract and regulate capillary blood flow?

options.explanation: Pericytes (Rouget cells) are contractile cells that wrap around capillaries and post‑capillary venules.
Endothelial cells are not primarily contractile.
Fibroblasts produce ECM.
Mesangial cells are in the glomerulus, not typical capillaries.
Myofibroblasts appear in wound healing.

explanation.overview: Pericytes have contractile properties and can regulate microvascular blood flow.
explanation.highYield: Pericytes = contractile, capillaries.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Pericyte loss in diabetic retinopathy leads to microaneurysms.

questions.question: The arterial supply to the walls of large arteries is provided by:

options.explanation: Vasa vasorum are small vessels that penetrate the adventitia and outer media.
Diffusion is insufficient for thick-walled arteries.
Lymphatics drain, not supply.
Not the specific term.
Coronary arteries supply the heart.

explanation.overview: Vasa vasorum nourish the outer layers of large vessels.
explanation.highYield: Vasa vasorum = vessels of the vessel.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Occlusion of vasa vasorum may contribute to aortic dissection.

questions.question: Which of the following is a feature of fenestrated capillaries in the intestinal villi?

options.explanation: Fenestrated capillaries in the gut have diaphragms across the pores, unlike glomerular capillaries.
That's continuous capillaries.
That's sinusoidal.
That's glomerular capillaries.
Capillaries lack smooth muscle.

explanation.overview: Fenestrated capillaries with diaphragms facilitate absorption.
explanation.highYield: Intestinal villi: fenestrated with diaphragms.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: These capillaries absorb nutrients.

questions.question: The muscularis of the heart (myocardium) is thickest in which chamber?

options.explanation: The left ventricle has the thickest myocardium to generate high pressure for systemic circulation.
Thinner than left ventricle.
Thin walled.
Thin walled.
They differ.

explanation.overview: The left ventricle pumps against the highest pressure.
explanation.highYield: Left ventricle = thickest myocardium.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Left ventricular hypertrophy in hypertension.

questions.question: What type of epithelium lines the surface of the epicardium?

options.explanation: The epicardium is covered by mesothelial cells, a simple squamous epithelium.
Not cuboidal.
Not.
Not.
Not.

explanation.overview: The epicardium is the visceral layer of the serous pericardium, lined by mesothelium.
explanation.highYield: Epicardium = simple squamous mesothelium.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Mesothelioma can arise from mesothelium.

questions.question: What is the functional significance of the numerous elastic lamellae in the aorta?

options.text: Allow distension during systole and recoil during diastole
options.explanation: Elastic fibers store energy, maintaining diastolic pressure and smoothing blood flow.
They reduce resistance by dampening pulsatility.
Not the function.
Elastic arteries have less smooth muscle than muscular arteries.
Endothelium does that.

explanation.overview: Elastic arteries act as pressure reservoirs (Windkessel effect).
explanation.highYield: Aorta elasticity → Windkessel effect, continuous flow.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Arteriosclerosis reduces compliance, increasing pulse pressure.

questions.question: Which of the following vessels has the smallest total cross-sectional area in the systemic circulation?

options.explanation: The aorta has the smallest total cross‑sectional area; capillaries have the largest total area despite individual small diameter.
Collectively, capillaries have the largest cross-sectional area.
Larger than aorta.
Total cross-section larger than aorta.
Greater total area than aorta.

explanation.overview: Cross‑sectional area inversely correlates with blood velocity.
explanation.highYield: Aorta = smallest total cross‑sectional area, highest velocity.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Aortic stenosis reduces effective orifice area.

questions.question: Which of the following is characteristic of the atrioventricular node histologically?

options.text: Small cells with few gap junctions, embedded in fibrous tissue
options.explanation: The AV node has small, pale nodal cells similar to SA node but with more connective tissue, causing slow conduction.
Purkinje cells are in the ventricles.
Not typical.
No.
Contains nodal cells.

explanation.overview: The AV node delays the impulse to allow ventricular filling.
explanation.highYield: AV node = small, pale cells, fibrous tissue, slow conduction.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: AV nodal block can cause bradycardia.

questions.question: Which of the following vessels is responsible for the majority of peripheral resistance?

options.explanation: Arterioles have the greatest ability to regulate resistance due to their muscular walls.
Capillaries have no smooth muscle.
They distribute but arterioles are the main resistance vessels.
Venules are low resistance.
They have low resistance.

explanation.overview: Arterioles are the primary resistance vessels regulating blood pressure and local flow.
explanation.highYield: Arterioles = resistance vessels.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Antihypertensives target arteriolar tone.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the arrangement of smooth muscle in the tunica media of arteries?

options.explanation: Smooth muscle cells are arranged concentrically around the lumen.
Longitudinal smooth muscle may be in veins.
Not random.
Spiral arrangement exists but circular is the typical description.
Present.

explanation.overview: Circular smooth muscle constricts the lumen.
explanation.highYield: Arterial smooth muscle = circular.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Vasospasm involves intense contraction of this layer.

questions.question: Which of the following is a feature of the splenic red pulp cords?

options.text: Reticular fibers, macrophages, and extravasated blood cells
options.explanation: Cords of Billroth consist of a meshwork of reticular fibers and macrophages through which blood percolates.
Follicles are in white pulp.
Sinuses are between cords.
No smooth muscle in cords.
T cells in PALS.

explanation.overview: Red pulp cords filter blood, removing aged erythrocytes and pathogens.
explanation.highYield: Cords of Billroth = reticular fibers + macrophages.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Congestion of red pulp occurs in splenomegaly.
